title: Fibres of the affine groupoid invariant spectrum are orbits
statement: Let $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ and $R=\operatorname{Spec}B$ be affine schemes [def-pc-scheme], [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Suppose $s,t:R\to U$, $e:U\to R$, $i:R\to R$ and $c:R\times_{s,U,t}R\to R$ [def-pc-fibre-product] are morphisms such that, functorially in every test scheme $H$, $U(H)$ is the object set and $R(H)$ the arrow set of a groupoid with source $s$, target $t$, identity $e$, inverse $i$ and composition $c$. Write $\sigma=s^\sharp,\tau=t^\sharp:A\to B$ and $C=\{a\in A:\sigma(a)=\tau(a)\}$. Assume $s,t$ are finite locally free [def-pc-finite-locally-free]. For $M=\operatorname{Spec}C$, the canonical map $|U|\to|M|$ is surjective. Two points $u_0,u_1\in|U|$ have the same image in $|M|$ if and only if there exists $r\in|R|$ with $s(r)=u_0$ and $t(r)=u_1$. Moreover, for every algebraically closed field $k$ [def-weil-algebraic-closure], the map $U(k)\to M(k)$ is surjective and its fibres are exactly the equivalence classes generated by $s,t:R(k)\rightrightarrows U(k)$.

proof.text: By [lem-a1-affine-groupoid-integral-invariants], $C\hookrightarrow A$ is integral; it is injective since $C$ is the displayed subring. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-integral-injective-lying-over] to obtain surjectivity on ordinary points. For an algebraically closed field $k$ and $d:C\to k$, lying over gives a prime $\mathfrak q\subset A$ over $\ker d$; [lem-dl-a1-integral-geometric-point-existence], applied to the integral map $C\to A$, to $\phi=d$ and to $\mathfrak q$, gives $a:A\to k$ extending $d$ (with kernel $\mathfrak q$). So the map on $k$-points is surjective for every algebraically closed $k$. The zero-ring case is included.

Fix $a_0,a_1:A\to k$ with common restriction $d:C\to k$. Apply [lem-a1-affine-groupoid-basechange-polynomial-norm] with $D=k$ to get the finite locally free groupoid on $A_k=A\otimes_Ck$, $B_k=B\otimes_Ck$. The maps $\alpha_j(a\otimes\lambda)=a_j(a)\lambda$ are $k$-algebra maps. Every $g=N_{\sigma_k}(\tau_k(f))$ lies in the scalar image of $k$, hence $\alpha_0(g)=\alpha_1(g)$. If no arrow joins $\alpha_1$ to $\alpha_0$, [lem-a1-affine-groupoid-norm-prime-separation] supplies $f$ for which this same norm satisfies $\alpha_0(g)=0\ne\alpha_1(g)$, a contradiction. Thus such an arrow exists.

Restrict its map $B_k\to k$ along $B\to B_k$ to get an original arrow from $a_1$ to $a_0$. Conversely an arrow $\gamma:B\to k$ whose endpoints restrict to $d$ extends by $b\otimes\lambda\mapsto\gamma(b)\lambda$. Every arrow preserves the restriction to $C$, since $\sigma|_C=\tau|_C$. Identity, inverse and composition make the one-arrow relation reflexive, symmetric and transitive, so it equals the generated equivalence relation. Inversion gives the desired endpoint order. This proves the geometric fibre assertion.

For ordinary points $u_0,u_1$ above $m$, with prime $\mathfrak p\subset C$, let $k$ be an algebraic closure of $\kappa(m)$ [def-weil-residue-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure] and $\phi:C\to\kappa(m)\to k$; its kernel is $\mathfrak p$. Since $C\to A$ is integral (step 1) and both primes $u_j$ contract to $\mathfrak p$, [lem-dl-a1-integral-geometric-point-existence] gives maps $a_j:A\to k$ extending $\phi$ with kernels $u_j$, so with equal restrictions to $C$. Steps 2-3 give a $k$-arrow; its underlying point $r\in|R|$ has endpoints $u_0,u_1$, as follows by taking inverse images of its kernel under $\sigma,\tau$. Conversely any $r$ has endpoints with the same image in $|M|$, because the two homomorphisms $C\to B$ agree. Together with step 1, this proves the ordinary fibre assertion.
